simple_explanation: The amount you pay to keep an insurance policy active.
Money that has not yet been paid.
An extra charge for paying after the deadline.
Extending a service, policy, or agreement for another period.
The ending of an agreement or service.
The amount of time one side must give before a change or cancellation takes effect.
The conditions someone must meet to qualify for something.
A request to have a decision reviewed again.
The last day by which a payment should be made.
The regular period, such as a month, that a bill covers.
The smallest payment you must make by the due date to avoid a late fee.
Past the date by which payment or action was expected.
A summary of your transactions and balance over a period of time.
A document listing what you were charged for and how much you owe.
Equated Monthly Instalment: a fixed amount you pay every month to repay a loan.
An extra charge for borrowing money, or a reward for keeping money in an account.
The original amount of a loan, not counting interest.
The maximum amount you are allowed to borrow or spend on a credit card.
Spending more money than your account holds, which the bank covers for a fee or interest.
The least amount of money you must keep in your account to avoid a penalty.
An arrangement that lets a company take payments from your bank account automatically.
A permanent order to your bank to make a payment automatically at regular intervals.
A reversal of a card payment after you dispute it with your bank.
A charge for restoring a service, such as electricity or internet, after it was cut off.
Money held as a guarantee, usually returned if you meet the terms.
Money that should have been paid earlier but is still unpaid.
Know Your Customer: the process of verifying your identity and address with a bank or service.
A warning that a service will be stopped if you do not pay or act by a certain date.
The set of rates or prices charged for a service.
Extra fees for using a mobile network outside your home area.
The written agreement between you and an insurer that sets out what is covered.
The maximum amount an insurer will pay out under your policy.
A request to your insurer to pay for a loss or expense covered by your policy.
The part of a claim you must pay yourself before the insurer pays the rest.
A fixed share of the cost of a claim that you pay and the insurer does not.
The time after buying a policy before certain benefits can be claimed.
Extra time after the due date during which you can still pay without losing cover.
When a policy ends because the premium was not paid in time.
Something your policy does not cover.
The person you choose to receive the benefit of a policy if something happens to you.
A claim where the insurer pays the hospital directly, so you do not pay upfront.
A claim where you pay first and the insurer pays you back afterwards.
A discount or extra cover given for a year in which you made no claims.
A document confirming that your policy is active and showing its period of cover.
A health problem you already had before buying the policy.
A single numbered part of a contract that covers one specific point.
A person or organisation that signs a contract.
Legal responsibility for loss, damage, or debt.
A promise to cover someone else's loss or damage.
Failing to follow a term of an agreement.
An unexpected event outside anyone's control, such as a flood, that excuses a party from the contract.
A duty to keep certain information private.
A written change made to an existing agreement.
A way of settling a dispute by a neutral person instead of going to court.
A set time during which you cannot cancel an agreement without a penalty.
The specific things one side has agreed to provide under a contract.
A person who watches a document being signed and signs to confirm it.
Being accepted into a college or course.
A document that allows you to enter an examination hall.
A request to have your exam answers checked again.
A temporary certificate issued until the final one is ready.
Money given to a student to help pay for education.
An official notice sent to many people at once.
Confirmation by an authorised person that a copy is a true copy of the original.
A copy of a document that you have signed yourself to say it is a true copy.
An official announcement of a rule, date, or decision.
A formal complaint about unfair treatment or a service problem.
A document proving that you live permanently in a particular state.
A document stating that an organisation has no objection to what you plan to do.
